title: The sky is blue, not violet, partly because of your eyes
body: Sunlight contains every colour, but the nitrogen and oxygen molecules in air scatter short wavelengths far more strongly than long ones: the effect grows as one over the wavelength to the fourth power, so blue light at 450 nm scatters about **6 times** more than red at 700 nm. That scattered light reaches us from every direction, so the whole sky glows blue. Violet scatters even more, yet the sky doesn’t look violet; part of the answer is that sunlight holds less violet and our eyes are less sensitive to it. At sunset the light crosses much more air, so most of the blue is scattered away before it reaches us.

slides.question: Air scatters blue light (450 nm) more than red (700 nm). About how many times more?
slides.explanation: About 6 times: scattering grows as one over the wavelength to the fourth power, and (700 ÷ 450) to the fourth power is about 5.9.

slides.alt: Animation over dark hills from dawn to sunset: coloured light waves stream from the Sun, and air molecules bounce blue and violet waves around far more than red, turning the sky blue. Bars show the fourth-power rule, then a diagram shows the long sunset path through the air.

slides.heading: How strongly air scatters each colour
slides.note: Relative to red, from the fourth-power rule

slides.heading: So why not violet?
slides.text: Violet scatters most of all. Part of the answer, says the [Physics FAQ](https://math.ucr.edu/home/baez/physics/General/BlueSky/blue_sky.html), is that sunlight holds less violet and our eyes are less sensitive to it. Our eyes take the scattered mix as blue blended with white: a soft sky blue.

slides.heading: Sunsets flip it
slides.text: Near the horizon, sunlight crosses far more air. Most of the blue is scattered out along the way, leaving the oranges and reds of sunset.

slides.question: Why do sunsets look orange and red?
options: The Sun gives off redder light at dusk
Most blue is scattered away en route
Our eyes tire of blue by evening
slides.explanation: Near the horizon, sunlight crosses far more air, so most of the blue is scattered out along the way, leaving the oranges and reds.

slides.heading: Named after Lord Rayleigh
slides.text: The effect is called Rayleigh scattering, after the British physicist Lord Rayleigh (John William Strutt), who published papers on the colour and polarisation of skylight in 1871.
